nameStory: The "ruffled freckled pelt" gets its colorful name from its distinctive appearance - it looks like an animal pelt with a bumpy, textured surface covered in small spots or "freckles." The "ruffled" part comes from its wavy, crinkled edges that give it a rumpled fabric appearance, quite different from the smooth pelts of its relatives.
description: Ruffled freckled pelt lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms spreading patches on soil and moss. Like other pelt lichens, it has a distinctly two-sided appearance with different colors on top and bottom surfaces. This species is notable for its textured, bumpy upper surface that's dotted with small raised spots, giving it that "freckled" look. It's a medium-sized lichen that can spread several inches across in mature colonies.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels distinctly bumpy and textured to the touch, covered with small raised spots or "freckles" that create a rough, pebbled feeling unlike smoother pelt lichens

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms leafy, spreading patches with distinctly wavy, ruffled edges that curl and crinkle like wrinkled fabric rather than lying flat

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to brownish-green on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; underside is typically pale with darker veins

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows directly on soil, moss, or among low vegetation, never on tree bark or rock surfaces

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can reach several inches long, with colonies spreading up to 6-8 inches across in well-established patches

habitat: Look for ruffled freckled pelt lichen in moist, shaded areas with rich soil, particularly in deciduous and mixed forests. It thrives in areas with good air quality, often growing on moss-covered soil, forest floor humus, or among low vegetation in partially shaded clearings. This species prefers stable, undisturbed sites with consistent moisture levels.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant and easiest to spot as spring moisture brings out the green colors. The textured surface is particularly noticeable when damp from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more grayish during dry spells, but the distinctive bumpy texture and ruffled edges remain constant identification features.
seasonality.fall: Often becomes more visible again with increased moisture, and the freckled texture stands out well against fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover, appearing brownish-gray but retaining its characteristic rough, bumpy feel when touched.

funFact: This lichen is actually three organisms living together as one - it contains both green algae (Coccomyxa) and blue-green bacteria (Nostoc) as partners with the fungus, making it a rare example of a three-way biological partnership that's been successful for millions of years!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with freckled pelt lichen (Peltigera aphthosa), but ruffled freckled pelt has more pronounced wavy, crinkled edges and a distinctly bumpier texture - think "rough sandpaper" versus "smooth leather." The ruffled edges are your best field mark for telling them apart.
contextualKnowledge: The "pelt" in the name refers to animal hide or fur, which these lichens resemble when spread out flat. Early naturalists thought the two-toned, flexible appearance looked remarkably like tanned leather, leading to the common names we still use today.
compareHints: Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges. Dog pelt lichen and freckled pelt lichen are smoother to the touch, while scaly pelt lichen has a different type of surface texture with actual scales rather than bumps. The combination of pronounced ruffling and pebbly texture makes this species quite distinctive once you know what to feel for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
